title: Social-Media Management
subtitle: Help a local business show up clearly without living on your phone.

blocks.text: A shop owner can fix a bike and still run out of time to post before closing. Social-media management turns that unfinished task into a clear service you sell. Your phone can help you work, but it does not need to become your new boss.
Start with one clear offer.
blocks.detail: A small, written scope helps you finish good work and protect your time, even when the client has another great idea.
blocks.extra: Section 02 shows you how to build and price that offer.

sections.title: Start with a service you can explain

blocks.text: A social-media manager helps a business plan and make posts, get them approved, publish them and handle agreed replies. The manager also reports what happened. A small agency can begin with one person serving one client well.

Your client keeps control of the business account and its promises to customers. Your job is to make good, true information easier to find. Start with one local bike repair shop and one channel, rather than offering every platform.
Agree on the work before you make content. A useful first offer lists the number of posts, how many rounds of changes, your reply hours and who approves each post. It also says what costs extra.

items.title: PRICE THE PILOT
items.text: Count your hours for planning, writing, photos, edits and replies. Multiply by the hourly rate you need, then add a buffer for back-and-forth. Quote one flat price for the pilot.

items.title: PUT IT IN WRITING
items.text: Send a one-page agreement: posts and dates, rounds of changes, reply hours, who owns the files, how either side can end the work, and when you get paid.

items.title: KEEP AD MONEY APART
items.text: If the owner runs paid ads, the ad budget is theirs and gets billed to their card. Your fee is for your work only.

sections.title: Build a client workflow that holds up

blocks.text: Begin with a short intake form. Ask who the shop serves, which services it wants to explain and where customers already look for news. In our example, the owner picks its existing Facebook page, because customers ask about repair hours there.

items.title: Collect approved hours, service details, booking links and the shop’s tone of voice.
Agree on four posts over two weeks, one revision round and weekday reply checks.
Name one approver and set an approval deadline. Silence means the post waits.
Write down the topics you can answer and the issues the owner must handle.

blocks.text: Keep one facts sheet with the date the owner last confirmed it. A price list from last spring may be a lovely piece of history and a poor guide to today’s prices.

Canada’s Cyber Centre says each person should get their own access, not a shared password. Ask for a page role that gives only the access you need, turn on two-step login, and leave account recovery with the owner.

Check that you may use the logo, photos, music and other content. Do not assume an image found online is free to reuse. The Privacy Commissioner says consent should explain why you collect, use or share someone’s personal information. Ask clearly before you feature a customer people can recognize.
Set reply limits in writing. Answer routine questions about hours with approved wording. Send refunds, repair safety concerns and complaints to the owner. Keep customer details out of public replies.

items.title: “Managing social media means being available all day.”
items.text: Reply hours are part of the agreement. A public note on response times tells customers when to expect a reply, and urgent issues follow a separate plan to reach the owner.

blocks.text: Keep a dated record of approvals and the posts that went live. When the work ends, return the agreed files and reports. Then have the owner remove your page role and your access to any scheduling tool.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: The Saturday repair post

blocks.text: The Saturday repair post
paragraphs: Danielle lived in Regina and worked part-time at a shop. She wanted a first social-media client who fit around that job. A small bike repair shop needed help before the busy riding season. She offered a two-week trial and set aside two evenings a week.

Her first post promised Saturday tune-ups with same-day pickup. The owner had said Saturdays were busy, and Danielle had guessed the rest. When she sent the posts for approval, the owner flagged it. The mechanic could not promise same-day work.

The post was due the next morning. Danielle worried that a delay would make her look slow. She thought about changing one word and posting it anyway. Instead, she held the post and asked what customers could book on Saturdays.

Together they swapped the promise for clear drop-off and booking steps. Danielle added the new wording to her facts sheet and sent the posts back for approval. She also spotted a customer’s phone number in a work-order photo and cropped it out.

In week two, the clearest post got fewer likes than the bike photo. But three people asked how to book a repair, and the owner confirmed one booking from those chats. Danielle reported those numbers on their own. She did not claim every question became a sale.

The owner liked the approval steps but could only review posts on Thursdays. Danielle moved her draft deadline to Tuesday and offered a plan for the next month. Her two evenings stayed on the calendar, and the Saturday promise stayed out of the posts.

blocks.text: This made-up trial shows what the process can teach. The caught promise and the customer questions point to fixes; neither predicts another client’s results.
Build trust through the process.
blocks.detail: A clear approval routine helps you catch mistakes early and gives the client a good reason to keep working with you.
blocks.extra: Section 05 walks you through a full two-week batch.

sections.title: Walk through a two-week content batch

blocks.text: This sample trial is an example, not a required package. Prepare four posts: how to book, a service explained, a workbench photo staff approved, and a reminder of current hours. Give each post one purpose and a clear next step.

items.title: Make a batch sheet with the draft text, image, facts checked, approver, status and planned date.
Check each image for customer details and permission to use it.
Send the complete batch on Tuesday; ask for approval by Thursday.
Revise the batch once, record approval and schedule only approved items.
Check replies during the agreed weekday hours and log every issue sent to the owner.

blocks.text: Use an approval queue with simple labels: Draft, Needs change, Approved and Posted. A post marked Needs change cannot jump to Posted just because its time slot is close.

Make the posts easy for everyone to use. W3C, the web standards group, advises adding alt text that says what an image shows. Describe the workbench scene where the platform allows it. For video, add captions, check any automatic captions, and put the key booking details in the post text too.

Use clear lettering with strong contrast against the background. Read each post on a phone before you send it for review. A booking link should still make sense without anyone zooming in on a tiny graphic.

items.title: “A public post and a sales DM follow the same rules.”
items.text: The CRTC says a public post on a Facebook wall is not covered by Canada’s anti-spam law (CASL), but direct messages can be. A sales message sent that way generally needs consent, the sender’s name and contact details, and a way to unsubscribe.

blocks.text: The Competition Bureau says false or misleading promotions break the law. Check claims about prices and timing. Use only real reviews, with permission. Avoid fake followers, copying people’s contact details from other sites, and mass sales messages.
Keep paid ads separate. An ad budget the owner approves is not your fee, and a trial does not promise reach, bookings or sales.

Insider tip: Build a one-page monthly report from your log: posts delivered, clicks on the booking link, real customer questions, bookings the owner confirmed, and issues solved. Note the dates and the limits of the data. Follower growth alone does not show what customers did.
Quick Check

items.title: Who approves a post that changes the shop’s service promise?
items.detail: The named client approver confirms it before publication.

items.title: Does a growing follower count prove the shop gained sales?
items.text: Track relevant inquiries and owner-confirmed outcomes separately.

items.title: What should happen to your account access when the service ends?
items.detail: The owner revokes your role and any connected tool permissions after the agreed handover.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Your post promises same-day repairs, but the owner has not approved it. What should you do? A. Publish to meet the schedule. · B. Hold it and confirm the wording. · C. Add a small disclaimer after publishing.
items.text: Publication waits for approval, especially when a post makes a service promise.

items.title: A customer posts a phone number beside a complaint. What is the best response? A. Repeat the number to show you noticed. · B. Promise a refund. · C. Follow the privacy and escalation plan without repeating personal details.
items.text: Protect customer details and send complaints beyond your authority to the owner.

items.title: The client offers its password. What is the better setup? A. Use your own authorised role with suitable permissions and two-factor authentication. · B. Keep the password in a shared draft. · C. Ask every helper to use the same login.
items.text: Individual role access supports control and a clean handover when your work ends.

items.title: Written: Describe two measures for a monthly bicycle-shop report and explain what each tells the owner.
items.text: Relevant repair inquiries show customer interest. Owner-confirmed bookings show a later action; neither proves that all interest turned into sales.

blocks.text: Sell a defined service with client approval built in. Keep access secure, reply within agreed limits and report actions that matter to the business.
Use a real prospect or a made-up bike shop. Answer these questions before you offer a trial, so the client can see what you will deliver and what you still need to confirm.
Write a four-post trial scope and mark where the owner approves. Add one routine reply you could handle and one issue you would send to the owner. Then fill in the form below.

items.title: Scope
items.text: The agreed work, its limits and the delivery dates.

items.title: Content batch
items.text: Several posts prepared together for review.

items.title: Approval queue
items.text: A list that shows which drafts are cleared to post.

items.title: Escalation
items.text: Sending an issue to the person who is allowed to handle it.

items.title: Alt text
items.text: A short text that says what an image shows.

items.title: Metric
items.text: A number you track to understand activity or results.

quiz.question: Your post promises same-day repairs, but the owner has not approved it. What should you do?
choices: Hold it and confirm the wording.
Add a small disclaimer after publishing.

questions: Which customer question will your first post answer?
Who will approve your posts, and by which day each week?
Which questions or issues will you always send to the owner?
How will you get access to the account?
What will you put in your monthly report?
What next step will you take, and when?
samples: Write one question, such as how to book a repair.
For example: the owner, every Thursday by noon.
For example: refunds, safety concerns and complaints.
For example: my own page role with two-step login, never a shared password.
For example: booking-link clicks, real customer questions and bookings the owner confirmed.
Name one step and a date, such as writing a four-post scope by Friday.
